target.title: RFC 0016: Command Catalog
target.body:
## What this RFC proposes

A read-only **Command Catalog** built from command information OpenClaw already owns. It compares two concrete public shapes without changing command execution, permissions, or policy.

### Option A: broader catalog

```text
openclaw catalog list
openclaw catalog audit
openclaw catalog test-matrix
openclaw catalog summary
```

This option joins CLI descriptors, routes, runtime/plugin commands, and selected command-like tool adapters, then adds operational lenses.

- [Upstream draft](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/100960)
- [Foundation](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/11)
- [Dynamic/operator lenses](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/12)

### Option B: narrower commands surface

```text
openclaw commands list
openclaw commands inspect <command-path...>
```

This option follows noun-based groups such as `plugins` and `skills`, stays command-owned, and excludes the aggregate audit/test/summary reports and ownerless tool adapters.

- [Commands list](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/24)
- [Commands inspect](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/25)

OpenClaw already has a Gateway `commands.list` RPC for agent-facing chat/native/skill/plugin commands. Neither option replaces that RPC; the RFC calls out the naming overlap and leaves future convergence explicit.

## Shared boundary

Both options are read-only views over existing registries. They do not dispatch commands or enforce policy. The proposed source metadata remains small: effect mode, optional risk/confirmation, and public/internal exposure where the owning registry knows those facts.

## Feedback requested

- Is the broader `catalog` boundary useful, or is `commands` cleaner and more familiar?
- Should command-like tools remain outside the initial command inventory?
- How should either option eventually relate to Gateway `commands.list` and live paired-node command declarations?
- Which JSON fields should be stable beyond schema version, identity, and provenance?

target.title: RFC: Readiness Providers and Hosting Profiles
target.body:
## Decision Requested

Should OpenClaw own a canonical readiness-provider contract and use built-in hosting profiles to compose provider criteria into named, release-tested support contracts?

This extends surfaces OpenClaw already owns: `openclaw.json`, Gateway startup, the plugin activation registry, `/ready` and `/readyz`, health, and status. It does **not** add a second config system, a policy engine, an OCC dependency, or a hosted-platform abstraction.

The proposal has separable layers: maintainers can accept the readiness-provider contract without every built-in profile, and built-in profiles without custom composition.

## The Concrete Gap

OpenClaw can run in containers today, but "the process is alive" is not the same as "this runtime shape is usable."

A container can start with a loopback-only Gateway. A full PVC can leave HTTP alive while workspace writes fail. A node controller can start before any approved target is connected. Existing lifecycle readiness is useful, but it does not name and continuously evaluate these support postures.

Hosts close the gap with startup scripts, baked config checks, and downstream-only endpoints. Profiles make the support promise executable:

```text
OpenClaw supports these runtime shapes.
Each shape has stable predicates and failure reasons.
Each release validates the built-in matrix.
A running instance reports which shape it selected and whether it satisfies it.
```

## Evidence From Existing Issues

| Issue | Operator symptom | Contract needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [#96084](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/96084) | `/readyz` remains healthy when a full PVC prevents workspace writes. | Required workspace evidence with stable full/read-only/timeout reasons. |
| [#78136](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/78136) | Docker remains ready while the command queue is draining and rejects work. | Admission/drain state in required readiness. |
| [#73652](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/73652) | Gateway accepts connections before internal startup is usable. | Truthful startup admission boundary. |
| [#78954](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/78954) | Plugin/channel startup can block usable core startup. | Required versus advisory conditions. |
| [#43886](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/43886) | Docker Gateway intended for LAN still listens on loopback. | Effective topology checks, not configured intent alone. |

These motivate reusable criteria. They do not each require a profile: generally applicable invariants extend default readiness; profiles are for distinct named support postures.

## Built-In Support Contracts

| Profile | Intended posture | Additional readiness signals |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local` | Default foreground/local runtime | Required config, workspace, and Gateway evidence; plugin activation diagnostics advisory. |
| `container` | Gateway directly reachable through a container listener | `ContainerStateReady`: effective local listener is resolved and non-loopback. |
| `reverse-proxy` | Gateway behind a trusted identity proxy | `TrustedProxyReady`: trusted-proxy auth has a user header and trusted source. |
| `node-mode` | Gateway/controller for one or more controlled targets | `NodePairingReady`, `ControlledTargetsReady`, `CommandApprovalReady`, `ControlChannelReady`. |

A profile describes ingress/runtime posture, not packaging. Docker behind an identity proxy selects `reverse-proxy`; directly exposed Docker selects `container`.

Selection is optional and uses normal startup precedence:

```text
openclaw gateway run --hosting-profile <profile>
OPENCLAW_HOSTING_PROFILE=<profile>
openclaw.json: hosting.profile
```

Startup flag > environment > config > `local`. Selection validates effective runtime; it does not generate, merge, or repair configuration.

## Canonical Ready Result

Every condition carries:

```text
type + status + requirement + reason + message
```

| Requirement | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `required` | `False` or `Unknown` blocks readiness and appears in `failures`. |
| `advisory` | `False` or `Unknown` appears in `advisories` without changing HTTP 200 to 503. |

Existing Gateway startup, channel, drain, and event-loop failures remain authoritative and are merged with profile failures. The same result is projected through `/ready`, `/readyz`, health, status summary, and `status --json`; unauthenticated remote probes retain their redacted shape.

The RFC source specifies strict config, condition/result types, transport projection, condition uniqueness, set semantics, stable reasons, non-contractual ordering, non-normative messages, redaction, and fail-closed internal-evaluation behavior.

## Extensible Without Redefining Support

Built-in profiles remain OpenClaw-owned and release-tested. Operators cannot remove or demote their criteria. A namespaced custom profile extends exactly one built-in profile and only adds criteria:

```json5
{
  hosting: {
    profile: "acme/managed",
    profiles: {
      "acme/managed": {
        extends: "container",
        requiredCriteria: ["plugin.storage.backend"],
        advisoryCriteria: ["plugin.metrics.exporter"],
      },
    },
  },
}
```

Plugins register self-describing, activation-scoped readiness providers:

```ts
api.registerReadinessCriterion({
  id: "backend",
  async check({ pluginConfig, signal }) {
    return (await probeBackend(pluginConfig, { signal }))
      ? { status: "True", reason: "BackendReady", message: "Backend is reachable." }
      : { status: "False", reason: "BackendUnavailable", message: "Backend is unreachable." };
  },
});
```

Core publishes `plugin.<plugin-id>.backend` and owns registry lifecycle, namespacing, enumeration, timeout, cache/coalescing, invalid-result, error, and missing-registration behavior. Every active plugin provider is evaluated and reported as advisory by default; plugins cannot make themselves required. Only operator config can promote one. Missing, timed-out, throwing, `False`, or `Unknown` required criteria block readiness with stable evidence.

Provider checks are observational: read-only, idempotent, concurrency-safe, cancellation-aware, and free of blocking synchronous I/O. Their descriptors and resulting conditions are enumerable through the pinned registry and detailed readiness/status surfaces.

This is OpenClaw-native: registration lives in the pinned `PluginRegistry`, and output flows through the existing readiness aggregator. No Lobster type, endpoint, header, policy dependency, or global evidence store enters core.

Support follows inheritance. OpenClaw owns and release-tests every built-in profile. A namespaced operator profile must extend one built-in and cannot weaken it, so it retains that supported baseline. OpenClaw can support failures in inherited criteria as the underlying built-in profile; the plugin or operator owns added provider semantics and the extension's additional support promise. V1 intentionally excludes profiles with no built-in baseline.

## Boundaries

- Existing installations select `local`; no profile is required.
- Profiles never generate or repair config.
- Doctor and policy may diagnose the result later but are not readiness dependencies.
- Built-in criteria work with no optional plugin installed.
- Docker/Kubernetes/systemd own retries, intervals, start periods, and supervisor timeouts.
- OCC may select a profile as desired state, but readiness remains in the runtime/data plane.
- AgentHarness event streams, channel traffic, assistant deltas, tool events, approvals, and patches do not enter this contract.

## Concrete Draft Stack

| Slice | Draft fork PR | Reviewed head |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local readiness surfaces | [PR 17](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/17) | `cefbe89976` |
| Built-in profile selection and predicates | [PR 18](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/18) | `c423b77720` |
| Node-mode readiness | [PR 19](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/19) | `0dc6c7184f` |
| Workspace writability readiness | [PR 22](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/22) | `5678370063` |
| Extensible criteria and operator profiles | [PR 23](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/23) | `990ab4808c` |
| Release conformance gate | [PR 21](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/21) | `8aa1abbcf9` |

PR23 adds the public plugin/operator facility and passes 99 focused plugin-registry, config, CLI, status-contract, and readiness assertions. Its first Codex review found the custom CLI-selection gap; after that fix, final full-facility exact-commit review found no remaining correctness regression. The small CI-closeout commit passed focused lint/tests; two commit-review attempts timed out without output.

The four built-in runtime slices compose one package-installed `hosting-profiles` Docker lane. PR21 selects that lane in non-advisory package acceptance. Its changed workflow assertion passes; the broader Windows tooling file has five unrelated Telegram shell/executable-bit fixture failures with 44 other tests passing.

Actual Docker execution of the newest workspace `tmpfs` failure/recovery scenario remains pending because Docker Desktop was unavailable. The deterministic scenario and release wiring are implemented, but no local or brokered runtime success is claimed yet.

## Follow-Ups

- Stable telemetry events and metrics for readiness transitions.
- Optional doctor/lint findings and repair recommendations for selected-profile config.
- A possible `openclaw ready` CLI wrapper if HTTP plus status/health is not sufficient.
- Whether non-plugin runtime drivers need a separate registration surface.

target.title: RFC: Claws
target.body:
## Summary

- Defines one Claw package as one complete new OpenClaw agent for one job.
- Makes `claws add` create a new `agents.list[]` entry and workspace; existing agent/workspace collisions fail closed.
- Uses grouped `agent`, `workspace`, `packages`, `mcpServers`, and `cronJobs` ownership boundaries.
- Keeps skills, plugins, MCP servers, heartbeat, and Gateway cron on their existing OpenClaw owner surfaces.
- Uses enclosing `package.json` plus authenticated publishing for package identity, version, and publisher ownership.
- Excludes models, providers, credentials, channel bindings, `agent.skills`, and generic connectors from the portable contract.
- Gates the draft CLI behind `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`; when disabled, the command is unregistered and absent from help and completions.

## Lifecycle and safety

The lifecycle is `add`, `status`, `update`, `remove`, and `export`. Read-only plans precede consented mutation. Unsupported, blocked, drifted, or ambiguous ownership fails closed.

Grouped update rebuilds its plan immediately before mutation, uses each owner's strongest compare-and-swap or convergence boundary, advances root provenance last, and compensates completed owners in reverse order. Uncertain config/Gateway calls and package installs without artifact rollback are reported as partial rather than cross-owner atomic.

## Control UI alignment

[openclaw/openclaw#103176](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/103176) remains the Control UI surface for plugin inventory, installation, enablement/disablement, removal, and curated MCP connector discovery. Claws add package references to the shared lifecycle model; removing a Claw releases its reference and does not silently uninstall a shared plugin or skill. A global plugin pinned to another version by a different Claw fails update closed.

Portable MCP declarations remain direct validated `mcp.servers` configuration and do not create a feed-backed connector identity or replace the Control UI's curated connector shelf.

## Implementation stack

The RFC now links the ordered eleven-PR OpenClaw stack:

1. [#101328](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/101328) grouped schema and add planning
2. [#101755](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/101755) agent/root install
3. [#101973](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/101973) managed workspace files
4. [#102228](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/102228) ClawHub packages and shared uninstall warnings
5. [#102296](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/102296) status/remove
6. [#102306](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/102306) export
7. [#102383](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/102383) Gateway cron ownership
8. [#102406](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/102406) stdio/remote MCP ownership
9. [#102427](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/102427) lifecycle diagnostics
10. [#102959](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/102959) grouped update planning
11. [#102982](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/102982) consented grouped update apply

## Validation

- `git diff --check`
- line-wrapping and rendered Markdown structure scan
- all linked PR heads, bases, titles, and open state verified live
- consistency review against Patrick Erichsen's product/schema boundaries and merged Control UI PR #103176
